title: Entities on top of Jobs + Burst
sub: An entity is an ID, data sits in chunks, logic lives in systems — and the same jobs and Burst do the work
cards/0/title: Entities is the data model; Jobs and Burst run it
cards/0/body:
The Entities package (1.x) does not replace Jobs and Burst — it sits on top of them. Jobs and Burst answer how to compute fast: worker threads and machine code. Entities answers where the data lives and who walks over it.

Three ideas:

An entity is just an identifier: an index and a version. It has no fields, no methods and no Transform. A component is a struct with data, struct … : IComponentData, with no behaviour. A system is the logic: every frame it picks the entities that have the components it needs and processes them, usually in a Burst-compiled job.

Since components are unmanaged structs, they go into jobs and through Burst without any of the caveats from earlier units.
cards/1/body:
An archetype is a unique set of component types. All entities with { LocalTransform, Velocity } share one archetype; add Health and it is a different archetype.

Entities of one archetype live in chunks of 16 KiB. Inside a chunk there is a separate tightly packed array per component type, plus an array of the entities themselves. That is exactly the SoA layout from the previous unit, not AoS — an array of structs where each entity would be one struct with all its fields. A move system walks the LocalTransform array and the Velocity array front to back without touching anyone else’s fields, and Burst can vectorize that loop.

How many entities fit in a chunk depends on the total size of the archetype’s components: a fatter archetype means fewer entities per chunk and more chunks. When an entity is removed, the chunk’s last entity takes its slot, so the arrays stay free of holes.
cards/2/q: Match each Entities term with what it is
cards/2/pairs/0/1: an ID: index and version, no data, no logic
cards/2/pairs/2/1: a unique set of component types
cards/2/pairs/3/1: a 16 KiB block: component arrays of one archetype
cards/2/pairs/4/1: logic that walks a query every frame
cards/3/q: A 256-byte component that the move system never reads is added to the unit archetype. What happens to the move system?
cards/3/options/0: Fewer units fit in a chunk, so it walks more chunks, but those 256 bytes never enter the cache while it reads LocalTransform
cards/3/options/1: Every LocalTransform read pulls those 256 bytes into the cache too, as with an array of structs
cards/3/options/2: Nothing: component sizes do not affect chunks
cards/3/options/3: The system stops finding units: the archetype changed, so the query no longer matches
cards/3/explain: Inside a chunk every component has its own array, so a loop over LocalTransform and Velocity reads no foreign bytes — that is the SoA win. You pay differently: a fixed-size chunk holds fewer entities, and there are more chunks.
cards/3/wrong/1: That would be AoS — a single array of structs. In a chunk each component sits in its own array.
cards/3/wrong/2: A chunk has a fixed size, 16 KiB, so the fatter the archetype, the fewer entities it holds.
cards/3/wrong/3: A query requires components to be present, not an exact set: an entity with an extra component still matches.
cards/4/body:
A system in Entities 1.x is a partial struct … : ISystem with an OnUpdate(ref SystemState state) method. You can mark it [BurstCompile], and then OnUpdate itself is compiled by Burst.

A query says which components you need. SystemAPI.Query<RefRW<LocalTransform>, RefRO<Velocity>>() picks every archetype that has both components and walks their chunks. RefRW is read-write access, RefRO is read-only.

But a foreach over SystemAPI.Query runs on the main thread, as one loop. For tens of thousands of entities it is the same mistake as a loop in Update: the worker threads sit idle.
cards/5/title: IJobEntity: the same loop, as a job
cards/5/body:
IJobEntity is a job that Entities iterates for you. You write a partial struct with an Execute method, and the source generator builds a query from its parameters and expands it into a walk over chunks (the very IJobChunk).

In the parameters, ref means read-write and in means read-only. That is not style: it is how the system learns what it writes and what it reads, and how it builds dependencies. Execute is called once per entity that matches the query.

ScheduleParallel() spreads the chunks over the worker threads. In an ISystem, the call without arguments takes state.Dependency as its dependency and stores the new JobHandle back there, so you neither keep a handle nor call Complete(). Per-frame data goes in through job fields, as in any other job.
cards/6/q: What is true about IJobEntity? Select all that apply.
cards/6/options/0: ref on an Execute parameter means read-write, in means read-only
cards/6/options/1: The query is built from the Execute parameters
cards/6/options/2: The struct is declared partial: the source generator writes the rest
cards/6/options/3: In an ISystem you must call Complete() after ScheduleParallel(), or the next system reads half-written data
cards/6/options/4: Execute is called once per chunk
cards/6/explain: The Execute parameters define both the query and the access rights; partial is there for the generator. A system needs no Complete(): ScheduleParallel() without arguments puts the handle into state.Dependency, and a system that needs the same components gets it as a dependency. Execute runs per entity, not per chunk — per-chunk work is what IJobChunk does.
cards/7/q: Fill in the blanks: the job changes Shield, only reads ShieldRegen and runs in parallel on the worker threads.
cards/7/explain: partial is for the source generator; ref Shield — we write it; in ShieldRegen — we only read it; ScheduleParallel — over chunks on the workers. Run() would execute the job right away on the main thread.
cards/8/body:
If execution is the same, why Entities? Three things you would otherwise write by hand around bare NativeArrays.

Layout. The data already sits as SoA in chunks, and any new component lands in the right layout immediately.

Dependencies between systems. From ref/in (and RefRW/RefRO) Entities knows which types each system writes and reads. If one system writes LocalTransform and the next reads it, the second one’s state.Dependency already contains the first one’s job. That is “schedule early, complete late” for the whole frame: jobs chain onto each other with no Complete() in between.

Scenes and rendering. Subscenes, streaming, drawing — that is for the next lessons.

A caveat: a class component (a managed component) exists too, but it lives outside chunks and is not available to Burst or jobs. The fast path is struct only.
cards/9/task: Move the movement off the main thread. In MoveJob (IJobEntity) write Execute: LocalTransform for writing (ref), Velocity read-only (in), and the position moves by Velocity.Value * DeltaTime. In MoveSystem.OnUpdate replace the foreach over SystemAPI.Query with scheduling MoveJob via ScheduleParallel(), with DeltaTime = SystemAPI.Time.DeltaTime.
cards/9/checks/2/label: Execute moves Position by Value * DeltaTime
cards/9/checks/3/label: OnUpdate schedules the job with ScheduleParallel()
cards/9/checks/4/label: The system no longer loops over SystemAPI.Query on the main thread
cards/9/checks/5/label: No Complete(): state.Dependency carries the dependency
cards/9/explain: ref and in are both the access rights and the query: the job finds every chunk with LocalTransform and Velocity on its own. ScheduleParallel() hands the chunks to the workers and stores the handle in state.Dependency, so the next system that reads LocalTransform waits for it without a Complete(). In the interview: “a foreach over SystemAPI.Query is the main thread; for lots of entities, IJobEntity with ScheduleParallel”.
cards/10/q: Interviewer: “Is Entities faster than Jobs + Burst?” Which answer is accurate?
cards/10/options/0: The question mixes things up: the same jobs and Burst do the work. Entities is a data model: chunks with an SoA layout, queries and automatic dependencies between systems. The win comes from the layout and from all the logic becoming jobs
cards/10/options/1: Yes: Entities has its own compiler that beats Burst
cards/10/options/2: No: every entity is a heap object, so Entities is slower
cards/10/options/3: The same: Entities is a wrapper over GameObject and Transform
cards/10/explain: Entities does not execute code differently — it gives the data a layout Burst likes and builds the job graph between systems for you. If there is a single hot spot, Jobs + Burst over a NativeArray give nearly the same win without moving to Entities.
cards/10/wrong/1: Entities has no compiler of its own: systems and IJobEntity are compiled by the same Burst.
cards/10/wrong/2: An entity is not an object but an identifier; the data sits in chunks of unmanaged memory.
cards/10/wrong/3: An entity is not a GameObject and holds no Transform; position is a plain LocalTransform component in a chunk.
